MR Survey App

The numbers case study: survey experience redesign at scale for healthcare professionals: NPS from −13 to +44 between November 2024 and early 2026.

IN 10 SECONDS
PROBLEMSurveys carried heavy cognitive load, and respondents kept telling us (by email, with nothing measuring it) that the experience was poor. Respondents are also the supply chain, so a bad experience was a business risk.

Then a cognitive-load redesign led by the Patient Load survey, a verified onboarding flow, and a design system for 1,000+ surveys.
OUTCOMENPS −13→+44, Nov 2024 to early 2026 · +24% Patient Load completion rates · ~400→~550 MAU (+38%) · ~19% improvement in 90-day retention.

01Executive Summary

ZoomRx runs market research on healthcare professionals, physicians whose time is expensive, whose patience is short, and whose honest answers are the entire product. When I took on the survey experience, nothing measured it: feedback arrived by email, and nobody owned it. So the first thing I built was the measure itself, the Net Promoter Score (NPS) system, kept in an Excel sheet at first and later turned, with AI, into a dashboard anyone could open. Its first reading, in November 2024, was −13: respondents telling us, in the most direct metric that exists, that taking our surveys was a bad experience.

By early 2026, NPS was +44, a 57-point swing. None of that was one redesign; it was a sustained programme of experience work:

  • Reducing cognitive load, question by question
  • Rebuilding the feedback loops
  • Fixing onboarding
  • Building a design system that could hold quality steady across more than 1,000 live surveys

The measurement program linked detractor feedback to design sprints and contributed to NPS moving from −13 in November 2024 to +44 by early 2026. The NPS question and the end-of-survey feedback (EOSF) together collected 30,000+ structured responses. Patient Load completion rates increased by 24%; onboarding work grew monthly active users from ~400 to ~550 (+38%) and improved 90-day retention by ~19%.

02The world this product lives in

To judge the decisions you need the vocabulary they were made in. Healthcare market research is its own world; here is the plain-language version of the nine terms this case study leans on.

HCP panel
A standing community of healthcare professionals (physicians, mostly) who take paid market-research surveys for pharma clients. ZoomRx's panel is 60K+ HCPs and patients; the survey platform is where they meet it every day.
Panelist
A verified member of the panel. Identity is checked against a work email and an ID document before surveys unlock, because a research panel is only worth what its members' identities are worth.
Honorarium
What a physician is paid for a survey. It sits on every survey tile with the time estimate and "what you'll do", so taking a survey is an informed decision, not a gamble.
LOI
Length of interview: how long a survey says it will take, shown on its tile beside the honorarium. The usability study found surveys running longer than their advertised LOI, a broken promise to a physician who picked the survey partly on that number.
Screen-out
The qualification questions at the start of a study decide whether a respondent is eligible. Being screened out after fifteen minutes of qualifiers was the most-quoted frustration in the usability study.
Patient Load
The yearly onboarding survey every panelist completes about their practice. Its completion rate is one of the four numbers that moved: +24% year on year after the redesign.
EOSF
End-of-Survey Feedback: a two-step prompt at the moment a survey is completed, a recommendation score, then named areas of the experience to agree or disagree with. 30,000+ responses together with the NPS question; the programme's evidence base.
NPS
Net Promoter Score, from one question: "how likely are you to recommend us?", answered 0 to 10. Promoters answer 9 or 10, passives 7 or 8, detractors 0 to 6. The score is the share of promoters minus the share of detractors, so it runs from −100 to +100; passives count toward the total but neither add nor subtract. The platform's running measure: from −13 in November 2024 to +44 by early 2026.
SUS
System Usability Scale: a ten-question standard score where 68 is the benchmark. The study's SUS was 85, reassuring, and it hid the problem.

03Problem & Opportunity

A survey platform has an unusual property: its users are also its supply chain. If physicians dislike the experience, they respond less, answer worse, and eventually leave the panel, and the company's product (research data) degrades with them. When the first NPS reading came back at −13, it wasn't a vanity-metric problem; it was a leading indicator of supply risk. Demand for respondents had been growing faster than the panel, and the survey experience is where panelists spend nearly all of their time with ZoomRx, so the experience was the lever that decided whether the panel kept up.

The experience problems were structural. Surveys were long and cognitively expensive, dense grids, repetitive patterns, unclear progress. There was no systematic way to hear what respondents thought at the moment they finished. And with over a thousand live surveys authored across teams, quality varied wildly, the experience depended on who had built the survey, not on a system.

Design challenge

How might we make surveys that busy physicians don't dread, at a scale where no individual screen can be hand-polished?
RESEARCH & EVIDENCE
Methods
Moderated usability study: one-hour remote sessions with a discussion guide and four task scenarios on the live app, SUS, per-task errors, time and satisfaction, every session recorded · End-of-Survey Feedback (EOSF) built into every live survey · drop-off analysis by survey density · Amplitude funnel and cohort analysis · Jobs-to-be-Done framing for onboarding · design sprints prioritised from detractor feedback
Who we learned from
Eight panel physicians, oncologists and haematologists, recruited for paid one-hour sessions ($300 honorarium); task metrics from the seven who completed the task scenarios. Then the panel at large through 30,000+ NPS and EOSF responses, and the survey authors across the teams building the 1,000+ live surveys
Data
SUS (median 85) · errors, time and satisfaction per task · nine usability problems ranked by frequency and severity · weekly NPS · completion rate · monthly active users · 90-day retention · EOSF scores and free text
Not done, and why
Three of the six findings could not be fixed by design alone, who owns question design, the mismatch with how physicians remember interactions, and the burden of the check-in survey, and the study said so, in a section titled “where we need your help”. They went to the consulting and survey-programming teams; this programme took the other three and built the channel.
THE JOBS THE PRODUCT HAD TO DO
  1. Panel physicianWhen an invitation arrives between patients, I want the pay, the time and what I’ll be asked up front, so I can decide in seconds whether it’s worth it.
  2. Panel physicianWhen I’m mid-survey, I want to see how far I’ve got and never re-read a question, so finishing doesn’t feel like work.
  3. Panel physicianWhen I’m not going to qualify, I want to know in the first minute, and when I finish or get screened out, I want the next worthwhile thing in front of me.
  4. Survey authorWhen I build a new survey, I want the good version to be the default, so quality doesn’t depend on who built it.
  5. Research teamWhen a design changes, I want to hear what respondents thought at the moment they finished, so priorities come from evidence rather than opinion.

04Research: the study that started it

The study that started it

Before any redesign, we sat with the people taking the surveys. Eight panel physicians, oncologists and haematologists, were recruited for one-hour moderated remote sessions at a $300 honorarium and taken through a discussion guide and four task scenarios on the live app: sign-up, two survey flows, and the auxiliary flows around them. Every session was recorded; we measured errors, time and satisfaction per task and collected a System Usability Scale score.

Two kinds of numbers came out of it, and they disagreed. At the end of each session, participants filled in the System Usability Scale, a standard ten-question score out of 100 for how easy an app is to use. The median was 85, well above the 68 that counts as good, so on that score alone the app passed. The task timings said something else: the two survey tasks took eight to nine minutes each, averaged 1.4 to 1.6 errors, and were rated the least satisfying of the four tasks (5.3 out of 7). In plain terms, the shell of the app, its sign-up, navigation and account screens, worked well; the surveys inside it did not. The overall score was averaging the good part with the bad part, and hiding the bad part. That gap is the whole case study.

THE STUDY · AS RUN, NOT AS PLANNED
Method
Moderated usability study: one-hour remote sessions on the live app, with a discussion guide and four task scenarios, sign-up, two survey flows, and the auxiliary flows around them. Every session recorded.
Participants
Eight panel physicians, oncologists and haematologists, paid a $300 honorarium for the hour; task metrics from the seven who completed the scenarios.
Measures
Errors, time and satisfaction (out of 7) per task; a System Usability Scale score; nine usability problems ranked by how many participants hit them, with a severity out of five.
What we found
SUS median 85, above the 68 benchmark, while the two survey tasks took eight to nine minutes each, averaged 1.4–1.6 errors and drew the lowest satisfaction of the four (5.3 of 7). Surveys also ran longer than their advertised length (LOI), and respondents were screened out after fifteen to twenty minutes of qualifiers. The app was fine; the surveys inside it were not.
What it became
Six takeaways. Three were ours to fix and became Decisions 1, 2, 3 and 5; three (question ownership, the mental-model mismatch, the check-in survey's burden) went to the consulting and survey-programming teams, and the report said so in a section titled "where we need your help".

Six findings, ranked, and what each became

The sessions produced six takeaways and nine ranked usability problems, each with how many of the seven task participants hit it and a severity out of five. Three were ours to fix. The other three: nobody owning how questions are written and formatted, the mismatch between how physicians remember an interaction and how the survey asks them to report it, and the sheer burden of the check-in survey, needed the consulting and survey-programming teams, and the report said so in a section titled “where we need your help”. The table below is the traceability: which finding became which decision, and which ones honestly could not be solved by design alone.

In their words

05What the research said

Three things kept surfacing: in the sessions, in the task metrics and in the live surveys. Each one is tagged with where it was read from, and each became a decision.

01

The feedback had to come from the moment, not the memory

Asking respondents later what they thought produces politeness. Asking at the instant they finish a survey, while the friction is fresh, produces the truth. The End of Survey Feedback (EOSF) mechanism became the engine of the whole programme: 30,000+ responses, with the NPS question, that turned redesign priorities from opinion into evidence.

How we knewBefore the study there was no channel at all: panelists wrote emails, and with nobody owning them the emails went unanswered. Eight one-hour sessions were the first time the team sat with respondents, and what they said in the moment made the case for a permanent prompt at the end of every survey.→ Decision 1

Read from8 moderated sessions · the feedback emails nobody owned
02

Cognitive load is the real completion tax

Drop-off didn't correlate with survey length as much as with density, the grids, the repeated matrices, the screens that demanded re-reading. Reducing effort-per-question mattered more than reducing questions.

How we knewTask-based testing first: the two survey tasks took eight to nine minutes each with 1.4–1.6 errors and the lowest satisfaction (5.3 of 7) against a SUS of 85, the burden was in the questions, not the app. Then drop-off analysis across live surveys: completion fell with grid density and repeated matrices far more than with question count.→ Decision 2

Read fromerrors, time and satisfaction per task · drop-off analysis by survey density
03

At 1,000+ surveys, the system is the design

No team can hand-polish a thousand live instruments. Past a certain scale, the only way to raise experience quality is to raise the floor, tokens, patterns, and question templates that make the good version the default version.

How we knewThe study’s first finding: nobody owned how questions were formatted, a survey went from the consulting team’s draft to a coded instrument with no design step in between. Over a thousand live surveys had been authored that way, with quality varying by author.→ Decision 3

Read fromstudy finding 1: nobody owned question design · the 1,000-survey inventory

06Who I designed for

WHO I DESIGNED FOR · A COMPOSITE, NOT A PERSONA WITH A STOCK NAME
HCP
A panel physicianoncology and haematology in the study · verified panel member · takes surveys in the gaps of a clinical day, often on a phone
“I spend 15–20 minutes answering all these qualifications and then it says ‘sorry, you don’t qualify’. That’s demotivational and annoying.”
Goals
  • Decide in seconds whether a survey is worth it, pay, time and what I'll be asked, up front
  • See how far I've got and never re-read a question
  • Know in the first minute if I won't qualify, and what to do next
Frustrations
  • Fifteen to twenty minutes of qualification questions, then "sorry, you don't qualify"
  • A survey that runs well past the time promised on its tile
  • Dense grids and repeated matrices that demand re-reading, the burden was in the questions, not the app
  • Feedback sent by email, to nobody
Context & behaviour
Expensive time and short patience. Answers between patients, often on a phone. When the burden climbs, under-reports rather than abandons, and because the panel is also the supply chain, a bad experience degrades the data itself.
Composite of the eight study participants, the seven task participants' metrics and 30,000+ NPS and EOSF responses. Specialties and quotes are from the study; no names.

How might we…

  • HMW 1let a physician know in the first minute whether they'll qualify, and never leave them at a dead end?
  • HMW 2make a dense grid feel like four light steps, without cutting the questions a study needs?
  • HMW 3hear what respondents think at the moment they finish, instead of weeks later by email?
  • HMW 4make the good survey the default survey for authors who aren't designers?
  • HMW 5verify every identity without adding friction exactly where drop-off hurts most, at the door?

07Key Product Decisions

Decision 1: Build the feedback loop before the redesign

What we didn't do: redesign first and measure later, the instinct every team has when a number is bad.
What we saw

No channel existed. Panelists wrote emails, nobody owned them, and the eight sessions were the first time the team had sat with respondents.

What we did

Built the NPS and End-of-Survey Feedback system myself before redesigning anything, a score at completion, then a reason; an Excel sheet first, later a dashboard built with AI, and prioritised every sprint after from it.

The EOSF programme came first, deliberately. Redesigning on intuition risked optimising the wrong friction; 30,000+ responses meant every subsequent change had evidence behind it and a measurement after it.

Tradeoff: slower visible progress at the start, a quarter spent instrumenting instead of shipping screens. It converted the rest of the programme from guesswork to compounding.

The feedback data had a second life. The End-of-Survey Feedback and the emails before it kept raising the same questions: a survey link that would not open, a bonus that had not arrived, an account problem. So I designed and vibe-coded Zena, a support agent that lives on the dashboard: a panelist asks from the point they are stuck, Zena finds the survey, answers what it can about payments and surveys, and turns the rest into a ticket with the conversation attached. Its own card in More projects has the quick case study.

Decision 2: Attack cognitive load, not survey length

What we saw

The two survey tasks took eight to nine minutes with 1.4–1.6 errors; across live surveys, completion fell with grid density far more than with question count.

What we did

Targeted effort per question: simplified patterns, visible progress, dense grids broken into sequenced steps.

The redesign targeted effort-per-question: simplified interaction patterns, clearer progress, breaking dense grids into sequenced steps.

Tradeoff: sequencing dense questions adds screens and can lengthen perceived duration, the bet was that lighter screens beat fewer screens. The NPS trajectory and the 24% increase in Patient Load completion rates backed it.

Patient Load is where this decision is easiest to see. It is the yearly onboarding survey every panelist completes, and it had been losing completions year on year. The recording walks through the dense version first, then what we changed: guidelines before the first question, five steps by tumour group, indications chosen before the lines of therapy are asked for each one, and a visible path through all of it. Completion rose 24% year on year.

Decision 3: A design system sized for survey authors, not designers

What we saw

Nobody owned how questions were formatted; a thousand-plus surveys had been authored that way, quality varying by author.

What we did

A design system sized for survey authors: 200+ components, tokens and question templates that make the good version the default, no designer in the loop required.

The system's real users were the people building surveys at volume. It had to make the right pattern the easy pattern, templates and components that produce consistent experience without a designer in the loop. The system's rules are written doctrine, starting with its first principle: the physician is the hero; ZoomRx is the tool. Its discipline runs to the pixel, at one point, four visually indistinguishable navy variants that had drifted into production were consolidated into a single brand navy, on the record, with a date.

The Figma design system contains 200+ components, design tokens and WCAG 2.1 AA patterns for 1,000+ surveys across web and mobile. Its token architecture links primitive values to semantic roles and components; the source inventory also includes 439 icons and 249 illustrations. Later, the same system became the foundation for agent-generated screens, see the Boilerplate Generator case study.

Tradeoff: systematising removes flexibility, and some studies genuinely need bespoke instruments. The system had to leave escape hatches without letting the escape hatch become the norm.

The system, live

Below is the coded version of the design system, the one the Boilerplate Generator composes from, running on this page with its own tokens: 17 component recipes in three token tiers, primitive, semantic and component. Click through it; nothing here is a picture.

What the screen is made of

Decision 4: Onboarding as retention work, verification as trust work

What we saw

Amplitude funnel and cohort analysis on new panelists, framed with Jobs-to-be-Done; and a panel whose value rests on verified identities.

What we did

Redesigned onboarding around the jobs; verification with a work email from a persistent banner, surveys held blurred until the account is active.

Onboarding was redesigned using Jobs-to-be-Done and Amplitude funnel/cohort analysis. Monthly active users grew from ~400 to ~550 (+38%), and 90-day retention improved by ~19%. Identity also became part of the design: panelists verify with their work email and complete identity verification from a persistent dashboard banner, with surveys held blurred until the account is activated.

Tradeoff: verification gates add friction exactly where drop-off hurts most, at the door. But a research panel is only worth what its members' identities are worth: the friction buys the integrity the entire product is sold on.

Decision 5: Never dead-end a willing respondent

What we didn't do: end the experience at a thank-you page.
What we saw

"Fifteen to twenty minutes of qualifications and then sorry, you don't qualify", the most-quoted frustration in the sessions.

What we did

Every exit leads somewhere: finish → earnings and the next study; screened out → an apology with alternatives; home → the next opportunity waiting.

The survey loop is designed by scenario, and every exit leads somewhere: finish a survey and see your earnings and the next study ("Earn $75 more"); get screened out and land on an apology that immediately offers alternatives; head home and find the next opportunity waiting. A respondent with time and willingness is the scarcest asset the platform has; the design refuses to waste one.

Tradeoff: chaining opportunities risks feeling like a content treadmill. Pay, time estimates, and "what you'll do" sit on every tile so each next step is an informed choice, not an infinite scroll.

08Experience Design

The panelist's world

The dashboard is a working professional's earning surface, and it reads like one: survey tiles carry pay, time estimate, and "what you'll do" up front (respect for the respondent's decision, tile by tile) with early-access badges, guaranteed-pay variants, and honest unavailable states ("available again on…"). A verification banner tracks identity status at the top, and the platform's other faces sit one tab away: Surveys, Playground, Briefs.

Worth opening between surveys

A panel that only hears from you when you want data is a panel that stops answering. The platform earns visits between studies: clinical and case polls with community results, quizzes with explained answers, and the Playground, light engagement that keeps the habit alive without cheapening the professional context.

One ecosystem, visible in one screen

The dashboard quietly connects the portfolio: a $30 AI-moderated interview tile on it is Sagan, the interviewer I designed, being fielded through the survey platform, and the Briefs tab is Curie's content inside the panelist's daily surface. Three products from this portfolio, one screen.

09Directions I rejected

Four directions were on the table and were not taken. Each one was the easier build.

  • Redesign first, measure later.The instinct every team has when a number is bad. Redesigning on intuition risked optimising the wrong friction; the feedback loop came first and cost a quarter.
  • Shorten the surveys.Drop-off tracked density, not question count. The bet was that lighter screens beat fewer screens, and the studies kept the questions they needed.
  • A design system for designers.No designer was in the loop for most of a thousand surveys. The system had to make the right pattern the easy pattern for the people building at volume.
  • End at a thank-you page.A respondent with time and willingness is the scarcest asset the platform has. Every exit now leads to a next step.

10Validation & measurement

From a one-off study to a standing channel

The study was a one-off, and the thing it made obvious was that nothing continuous existed. Panelists had been writing emails; with nobody owning them, the emails went unanswered. So the first thing I built was the End-of-Survey Feedback prompt and the NPS system behind it, a recommendation score at the moment of completion, then a second step naming the areas of the experience to agree or disagree with, so a detractor score arrives with a reason. Design sprints were prioritised from detractor feedback, and NPS became the programme’s running measure, kept in an Excel sheet at first, later in a dashboard built with AI so anyone could open it: 30,000+ structured responses, from the NPS question and the end-of-survey feedback together, in the months that followed.

11Impact & Learnings

What changed in practice

The quality floor rose for every study ZoomRx fields, not just the ones a designer touched. And the platform became more than a survey queue: a verified professional community that earns, learns, and keeps coming back.

Honest limits on what I can claim

These are platform-level outcomes from a sustained team effort I drove the design of, not solo numbers.

Learnings I've taken forward

Instrument first, redesign second: a feedback mechanism built before the redesign multiplies everything after it.

At scale, the design system is the user experience. The most leveraged screen I designed was the template that shaped a thousand surveys I never saw.

01Executive Summary

Gribb's platform starts with a piece of hardware: a Geotab telematics device installed in delivery vehicles. It reports, live, how each vehicle is being driven, harsh braking, sudden acceleration, hard turns, idling, and more. For the delivery companies running these fleets, DHL and UPS among them, that stream holds the answers to expensive questions. Raw, it's unreadable.

As Lead Designer over 18 months, I designed both sides of that translation: the dashboard that fleet clients, insurers, and resellers used to understand every vehicle, driver, and trip, and the driver app that turned safe driving into a score worth competing for, with real rewards behind it.

The honest scope of this product is large: multi-tenant client management, a configurable rule engine, fleet analytics, fuel economics, exception maps, shift management, damage reporting, driver gamification. The design job was to make sure no single user ever felt that size:

  • A driver sees a score and a game
  • A manager sees their fleet and what needs attention
  • An insurer sees risk and evidence
The complexity lives in the system; the simplicity lives in each person's slice of it: keeping that separation was the work.

02Problem & Opportunity

A fleet operator cares about a small number of questions: who is driving dangerously, which vehicles need attention, and where the operation is losing money. The Geotab device answers all of them, but in the form of thousands of raw data points per vehicle per day. No operations manager at a delivery company reads telemetry, and no driver changes how they brake because a sensor logged an event.

The gap between what the device knew and what a client could act on: that gap was the product.

Design challenge

How might we turn one live telemetry stream into something two very different audiences act on, managers making decisions about their fleet, and drivers making decisions behind the wheel?

03Two seats, one engine

Told from both seats: the manager's and the driver's. Same telemetry, two working lives.

WHO I DESIGNED FOR · TWO SEATS, ONE ENGINE · ROLES, NOT INVENTED PEOPLE
OPS
A fleet operations manager at a delivery companyruns vehicles, drivers and shifts for a client such as DHL or UPS · answers to the operation and to its insurer · opens the dashboard first thing in the morning
DRV
A delivery driver on a shared fleetstarts a route on whichever van is free · judged by a score built from the device in the vehicle · rewarded, in gift cards, on how that score reads
Goals
  • Have anything wrong already in front of me when I open the dashboard, so I can act before the shift starts
  • See the trips and events behind a score, so I can defend it to the driver or correct it
  • Know whether the fleet is getting better, not only who needs attention today
  • Start a shift in seconds, without fighting a form
  • See my score and why it is what it is, on the trip, in the app
  • Stand somewhere against people I actually know, and have safe driving be worth something
Frustrations
  • Thousands of raw data points per vehicle per day that nobody reads
  • Serious incidents surfacing days later, in a report
  • Arguments over a score nobody can trace back to the road
  • Shifts that did not start in the app, so the record is wrong
  • A device that reports me upward to my manager; I never see what it saw
  • A number that judges me and cannot be questioned
  • A shared van with no record of who drove it, so a score with no owner
Context

Cares about a small number of questions: who is driving dangerously, which vehicles need attention, where the operation is losing money. Holds the operation accountable and has to show the client and the insurer evidence.

Changes how they brake because of a conversation with a manager, not because a sensor logged an event. Pushes back on numbers they cannot trace; every query raised in the field was a case where the score did not match the road.

Roles as the brief and 18 months of releases described them, not invented people. No interviews were run; what drivers thought comes from the queries they raised in the app, what managers wanted from the feedback behind each release.

How might we…

  • HMW 1turn one live telemetry stream into something two very different audiences act on, managers about their fleet and drivers behind the wheel?
  • HMW 2let a client define safe driving for its own roads, vehicles and weather, without a redesign for each one?
  • HMW 3make a score that judges people one they can contest, and still believe?
  • HMW 4make safe driving visible and worth something to the driver, not only to the manager?
  • HMW 5bind a driver to a shared vehicle in seconds, so per-driver scoring is possible at all?

04Fleet telematics in eight terms

Fleet telematics has its own vocabulary, and the decisions below were made in it. The plain-language version of the eight terms this case study leans on.

Geotab device
A telematics unit installed in each delivery vehicle. It reports, live, how the vehicle is being driven: harsh braking, sudden acceleration, hard turns, idling and more. Thousands of data points per vehicle per day.
Event
One thing the device noticed: a harsh-braking spike, a collision, idling past a threshold. People respond to events; nobody watches the stream they come from.
Exception
An event the rules decided was worth a manager’s attention. Exceptions surface on the dashboard and on a map; ordinary operation stays quiet.
Rule engine
Where events become a score. Every rule carries context: the same harsh braking scores differently on a snowy night in a truck than on a dry highway in a van. Road type, vehicle category, day versus night and weather are live, weighted inputs, and each client sets them from its own admin.
Driving score
The number the rule engine produces per driver, vehicle, trip and shift. Legible by design: every point traces back to a named rule, which is what lets a manager defend it and a driver contest it.
Query
A driver’s appeal against an exception, raised from the app with their case stated. The manager reviews the trip and marks it valid or invalid; valid queries correct the record.
Shift
The unit everything on the driver’s side hangs off. It starts with a scan of the vehicle’s number plate, which binds driver to vehicle and makes per-driver scoring possible on shared fleets.
Risk band
How a fleet is summarised for clients and their insurers: a weekly behaviour report that bands the fleet by risk, with exports and scheduled emails behind it.

05How we knew

There was no study to start from. This was agency work on a client’s roadmap, validated the way agency products are: in the field, one release at a time, with the CEO and CTO in the room. Who and what we learned from, the jobs it added up to, and what the field taught us.

RESEARCH & EVIDENCE
Methods
Working alongside Gribb’s CEO and CTO through 18 months of releases · client feedback on every version (Drivers v2 and v3, Trips V2, Check-in/out V2, Reporting v3) · driver queries from the live product, read as a research channel · the trip-lifecycle report, built to watch our own pipeline
Who we learned from
Gribb’s CEO and CTO, day to day · fleet clients (delivery operators including DHL and UPS, and insurers) through the feedback that shaped each release · drivers, through the queries they raised in the app
Data
Live telemetry events from the Geotab devices · driver queries and their valid / invalid outcomes · trip-lifecycle traces, device to dashboard · release-by-release client feedback
Not done, and why
No research phase before build, this was agency work on a client’s roadmap. The product was validated in the field, release by release, and the two channels above were built so the field could keep telling us.
THE JOBS THE PRODUCT HAD TO DO
  1. Fleet managerWhen I open the dashboard in the morning, I want anything wrong already in front of me, so I can act before the shift starts.
  2. Fleet managerWhen a score looks wrong, I want the trips and events behind it, so I can defend it to the driver, or correct it.
  3. DriverWhen I start a route on a shared van, I want check-in to take seconds, so the shift is recorded against me and not the last driver.
  4. DriverWhen I’m scored on my driving, I want to see why and to challenge it when it’s unfair, so the score is worth chasing.
  5. Client / insurerWhen I assess a fleet, I want evidence I can take out of the building, so risk-banding rests on behaviour, not claims history.
Worked through Jira across 18 months of releases (Drivers v2 and v3, Trips V2, Check-in/out V2, Reporting v3) and a full rebrand.
RELEASE BY RELEASE · WHAT THE FIELD TAUGHT US
Cadence
Five versioned releases (Drivers v2 and v3, Trips V2, Check-in/out V2, Reporting v3) and a full rebrand, worked through Jira. Each release was the test of the last one’s assumptions.
What we found
Managers and drivers needed the same data for opposite reasons. People respond to events, not streams. A score only changes driving if the people being scored accept it, and every query raised in the field was a case where the score did not match the road.
What it became
One data model with two faces (Decision 1), a rule engine configured by each client (Decision 2), due process for the score (Decision 3) and gamification with real stakes (Decision 4). Later releases added what clients asked for: shifts created on a driver’s behalf, a fleet-wide trend, day-wise reporting.

06What 18 months of releases said

Three things held across 18 months of releases. Each one is tagged with where it was read from, and each became a decision or a rule the whole product follows.

01

Managers and drivers need the same data for opposite reasons

A fleet manager looks at driving behaviour to hold the operation accountable. A driver looks at it to know how they're doing. One audience needs oversight; the other needs motivation. Designing one interface for both would have served neither, the data had to wear two faces.

How we knewWorked out with Gribb’s CTO from the two audiences’ jobs, the client’s fleet managers, who have to hold the operation accountable, and the drivers being held to it, and borne out by every release after: a metric added to the engine landed on both sides without rework.→ Decision 1

Read fromthe two audiences’ jobs, worked out with the CTO · every release after
02

Events matter more than streams

Nobody watches telemetry. People respond to things that happen, a collision, a harsh-braking spike, a vehicle trending toward a fault. The dashboard had to surface events and exceptions instantly and let ordinary operation stay quiet.

How we knewThe raw feed itself, thousands of data points per vehicle per day that no operations manager reads, and what clients were paying for: to know when something happened, not to watch a stream.→ the alert and exception model

Read fromthe raw Geotab feed · what clients were paying for
03

A score only changes driving if drivers accept it

A driving score changes conversations between managers and drivers, and drivers push back on numbers they can't trace. The score had to be legible (built from named events like harsh braking and idling, through rules anyone could understand) before it could be motivating. Gamification only works on top of a score people believe.

How we knewAnticipated with the CTO when the score was defined, a number that judges people invites pushback, then confirmed in the field: every query a driver raised was a case where the score did not match the road.→ Decision 3

Read fromthe score definition, with the CTO · driver queries in the field

07Key Product Decisions

The two hardest problems of the project sat next to each other: defining the rule engine, deciding how driving would be judged at all, and designing a dashboard that could hold this much product without collapsing. The gamification system and the plate-scan check-in were hard in a different way: they had to make sophisticated machinery feel effortless to the person using it.

Decision 1: One data model, two faces

The manager’s seat

Answers the manager’s questions: who is driving dangerously, which vehicles need attention, what the fleet looks like tonight. Framed for accountability.

The driver’s seat

Answers the driver’s: how am I doing, where do I stand, what’s my score. Framed for motivation, and always the same score the manager sees.

The client dashboard and the driver app were designed as one system serving opposite needs. The dashboard answers the manager's questions: who is driving dangerously, which vehicles need attention, what does the fleet look like tonight. The app answers the driver's: how am I doing, where do I stand, what's my score. Same telemetry, same rule engine, opposite framing.

Tradeoff: one coherent system is slower to design upfront than two independent products. It paid back constantly: every metric added to the rule engine appeared on both sides without rework, and the score a manager saw always matched the score a driver was chasing.

Decision 2: Configuration over customisation: the rule engine

What we didn't do: hard-code one universal definition of bad driving, the same thresholds for every client, vehicle, and weather condition. Far simpler to build, and wrong everywhere except the average case.
The manager’s seat

Each client sets the weights for road type, vehicle category, day or night and weather from its own admin, so the product holds its own definition of safe driving without a redesign.

The driver’s seat

The same brake is not the same brake: a harsh stop on a snowy night in a truck is not scored like one on a dry highway in a van, and every point traces to a named rule.

We didn't hard-code what "bad driving" means, because it doesn't mean one thing. Behaviour events flowed through a rule engine where every rule carries context: the same harsh braking scores differently on a snowy night in a truck than on a dry highway in a van. Road type, vehicle category, day versus night and weather were all live inputs, weighted, and configured by each client themselves from their own admin, down to the score bands and the colours that represent them.

Tradeoff: building the engine before the interface cost time when nothing visual existed to show for it, and every configurable option is a screen an admin has to understand. But it meant one product could serve every client's definition of safe driving without redesign, and the score stayed explainable, because every point traced back to a named rule.

Decision 3: Due process for the algorithm

The manager’s seat

Reviews the trip behind a query and marks it valid or invalid. The pattern of queries shows where the scoring feels wrong to the people being scored.

The driver’s seat

Can query any exception from the app and state the case: the speed limit was different, the idling had a reason. Valid queries correct the record.

A score that judges people needs a way to be wrong. If a driver believed an exception was unfair (the speed limit was different, the idling had a reason) they could raise a query from the app, state their case, and have it land with their manager, who reviews the trip and marks the query valid or invalid. Valid queries correct the record.

Tradeoff: an appeals process invites appeals, it costs manager time and admits the system makes mistakes. We took that cost deliberately: a contestable score gets trusted and a black box gets gamed. The dispute flow is what let the same number carry a manager's judgement and a driver's pay-adjacent rewards without being resented.

Decision 4: Gamification with real stakes

What we didn't do: ship the reporting-only version, telemetry flowing one way, upward to managers. It was the obvious MVP, and it would have made the app the driver's enemy on day one.
The manager’s seat

Gets a score drivers try to improve instead of resent, and one that is hard to game, because the rules are context-aware and every point can be contested.

The driver’s seat

Levels, streaks and milestones; leaderboards against people in the same hub; 30-second lessons that earn points; coins redeemed for real gift cards.

Surveillance data has a dignity problem: a system that only reports drivers to their managers gets resented and gamed. So the driver app flipped the framing. The score became a progression system (levels, streaks, milestones) with leaderboards ranked against people drivers actually know ("best 5% in your hub", not an anonymous global list), 30-second improvement lessons that themselves earn points, and coins that redeem into real Amazon gift cards.

Tradeoff: paying for scores invites chasing scores. The counterweight was the rule engine's context-awareness and the dispute flow, a score that's fair and explainable is hard to cheat and worth winning.

What we didn’t build

  • Two independent products.The obvious split: a dashboard for clients, an app for drivers. One coherent system was slower to design up front and paid back constantly: every metric added to the rule engine appeared on both sides without rework.
  • One universal definition of bad driving.The same thresholds for every client, vehicle and weather condition. Far simpler to build, and wrong everywhere except the average case.
  • A score with no appeal.A black box is cheaper than a dispute flow and gets gamed. A contestable score costs manager time and admits mistakes, and gets trusted.
  • Reporting-only telemetry.The obvious MVP: data flowing one way, upward to managers. It would have made the app the driver’s enemy from the first day.
  • An anonymous global leaderboard.Ranking drivers against strangers motivates nobody. The leaderboards rank against people drivers actually know: the best 5% in your hub.

08User flows: the app and the dashboard

The two products as people move through them. The driver’s flow hangs off the shift and ends in the game loop; the manager’s starts from whatever is wrong and drills down to a single event. The query is where the two flows meet.

09Experience Design

The shift is the spine

The driver's seat.

On the driver's side, everything hangs off one unit: the shift. Check-in by scanning the vehicle's number plate, the camera does the work, because a driver starting a route shouldn't be fighting a form. The check-in binds driver to vehicle, which is what makes per-driver scoring possible at all on shared fleets. Then the pre-vehicle safety check, the scored trips, any damage reports (tap the vehicle diagram where the damage is, add photos), and check-out. Each shift closes with its own score, its own condition record, its own paper trail, one driver, one vehicle, one accountable session.

The dashboard reads outward from the same spine

The manager's seat.

Fleet overview → vehicles → drivers → trips → exceptions, each level opening into the one below, down to a single braking event on a map. Around that core: live fleet map, fuel economics, score comparison between any two groups or periods, and reporting that leaves the building, exports, scheduled emails, and a designed weekly behaviour report that risk-bands the fleet for clients and insurers.

How every screen behaves

Two rules governed the whole product:

  • Problems find the manager, not the other way around. Open the dashboard and anything wrong is already in front of you; serious incidents interrupt with an alert, and everything running normally stays quietly in the background.
  • Every number opens up. Tap a score and see the trips behind it; tap a trip and see the events behind that. Nothing on screen is a dead end.

The same two rules hold on the driver's side: the score is always one glance away, and tapping it always shows you why it is what it is.

10The rebrand: identity, then the product

The product went through a full rebrand during those 18 months, and the branding was ours as well: the identity first, then the dashboard and the driver app carried over into it, so the two products read as one company.

11What shipped, and where it went

WHAT I CAN POINT TO
2 yrs
Lead Designer on the product
two designers, I led the design side
2 apps

5
Versioned releases
plus a full rebrand along the way
DHL · UPS
Among the clients
delivery operators and their insurers
2
Acquisitions since
Moove, then Netradyne: May 2026

Release by release

The product shipped in versions (Drivers v2 and v3, Trips V2, Check-in/out V2, Reporting v3) and went through a full rebrand along the way. Design here wasn't a phase before build; it was an 18-month loop of launching, getting feedback, and revising. The versions themselves show what that feedback taught us:

  • Check-in/out V2 added CSV shift imports and let managers create a check-in on a driver's behalf, because real shifts don't always start in the app. Drivers forget, and the record still has to be right.
  • Drivers v3 put a fleet-wide score trend graph above the driver list, managers weren't only asking "who needs attention today", they were asking "are we getting better?"
  • Reporting v3 went day-wise: weekly numbers were too coarse for clients who wanted to see the effect of a change that same week.

Two feedback channels were also built into the product itself:

  • Driver queries: every disputed exception told us exactly where the scoring felt wrong to the people being scored. The people most affected by the system were also its most honest testers.
  • The trip-lifecycle report: an internal screen we designed to watch our own data pipeline. It followed each trip step by step (from the Geotab device, into the backend, through scoring, to the result on the dashboard) and showed where a trip went missing or arrived late. So when a score looked wrong or slow, we could see exactly which step broke instead of guessing.

What changed in practice

Fleet behaviour stopped being invisible:

  • Every driver, vehicle, trip, and shift carried a legible score
  • Serious incidents interrupted instead of surfacing days later
  • Disputes were resolved inside the product instead of in arguments
  • Clients, and their insurers, received evidence: exportable reports and a weekly risk-banded behaviour summary

What had been a raw telemetry feed became the operating picture of the fleet.

The product also sold. The platform brought major delivery companies, DHL and UPS among them, and insurance companies on board as clients.

The market's verdict, though, is public. Gribb was acquired by Moove, the European connected-mobility group, and Moove has since become part of Netradyne, a global leader in AI-powered fleet safety. The premise survived two acquisitions intact. Netradyne's core pitch today (recognising and rewarding safe driving in real time, not just flagging what goes wrong) is the same bet this platform made in 2021.

Honest limits on what I can claim

This was agency-side work; post-acquisition usage data sits with Moove, Netradyne, and their clients. What I can speak to is the system's design logic and what I observed while building it.

Learnings I've taken forward

Data products fail at the interpretation layer, not the collection layer. The most valuable design work here wasn't visualising data, it was deciding what each audience needed the data to mean: accountability for the manager, motivation for the driver. Same numbers, two designs.

Bentley Mulliner

A real-time configurator for bespoke luxury vehicles, designed for iOS.

01Executive Summary

Bentley Mulliner is the bespoke arm of Bentley Motors. Customers don't pick from a catalogue; they specify a car. The existing iOS app, built to showcase the brand, didn't serve that decision: it described vehicles instead of helping anyone configure one.

I led the redesign from a static reference app into a real-time decision tool. Customers and Bentley executives could now build a complete specification, see it rendered immediately, and pass the result to a dealership for pricing. The work covered UX strategy, information architecture, high-fidelity design, and a rendering technique developed with engineering that gave us photoreal output without 3D, a constraint that ended up defining the product.

After launch, the app became the default surface for in-showroom configuration. Dealer follow-ups became structured rather than improvised: every build left the room as the same structured summary, ready for pricing.

02The decision at the table

For a Bentley buyer specifying a Mulliner build, the configuration moment is the most important decision of the purchase. Spec choices shift the price by significant amounts, and once committed, materials enter a production pipeline that takes months to reverse. The cost of a wrong call is high, both for the customer and for Bentley.

The original app was built to communicate craftsmanship, not to support that decision. It showed renderings of completed cars and reference imagery of trim options, but customers had no way to see their own combination. Reaching confidence required either imagination, picturing a colour from a swatch and a stitching pattern from a flat image and combining them mentally, or a multi-stop dealer conversation that often stretched across weeks.

What was broken

Dealerships were never under-equipped: physical swatches, material samples, and reference vehicles were all on the floor. What no showroom could offer was the customer's own combination, assembled: this colour on this body with this interior and this stitching. That composed view lived only in the customer's imagination, and confidence built slowly because of it. The digital experience, meanwhile, showed finished reference cars, it communicated the craft without supporting the decision in progress.

Design challenge

How might we let a customer specify a bespoke Bentley in real time, with enough visual confidence to commit, while staying within the performance ceiling of an iPad in a showroom?

The product moved from being a brochure to being part of the sales process.

03Three people, one iPad

The configurator sits between three parties. Two of them are in the room; the third receives what leaves it.

  • Be led through the choices in an order that makes sense

  • Pull up the customer’s build at the start of the next meeting

  • No composed view of the customer’s own car to point at

ONE IPAD BETWEEN THE CUSTOMER AND THE ADVISOR · ONE BUILD SUMMARY OUT OF THE ROOM

Roles from the brief, Bentley’s buyer data and the stakeholder reviews. We did not run sessions with end customers, so nobody is quoted.

04What we knew, and what we didn’t

The buyer side came to us as data, with the brief. Everything else was learned with Bentley: stakeholder sessions to understand the problem, workflow reviews with Mulliner-trained advisors, and variant comparisons inside the team. What we could not do, we say.

RESEARCH & EVIDENCE
Methods
Bentley’s own buyer data, which arrived with the brief as the problem statement · stakeholder sessions with Bentley to understand it · workflow reviews with Mulliner-trained sales advisors · internal usability walkthroughs of each prototype · side-by-side comparisons of interaction variants built within the team
Who we learned from
Bentley’s product manager, our client-side point of contact, and Bentley’s product stakeholders, including Mulliner-trained sales advisors. Not end customers: the buyer side came from Bentley’s data, not from sessions we ran.
Data
Bentley’s buyer data in the brief · what stakeholders and advisors told us about the showroom conversation · observation in internal walkthroughs and variant comparisons · the asset register: 1,500+ PNG layers positioned by hand
Not done, and why
No usability sessions with end customers: Bentley’s buyers weren’t ours to recruit, and the brief carried their data. No post-launch telemetry either: outside the contract, as the honest-limits paragraph says.
THE JOBS THE PRODUCT HAD TO DO
  1. CustomerWhen I’m choosing a finish, I want to see my combination on my car immediately, so I can commit with confidence.
  2. CustomerWhen I’m configuring, I want to be led through the choices in an order that makes sense, so I don’t get lost in options.
  3. Sales advisorWhen a customer is exploring, I want to step in at the right moments rather than narrate throughout, so the decision stays theirs.
  4. Dealership / productionWhen a spec is agreed, I want a build summary I can hand on without translation, so nothing is re-keyed or reversed months later.
  5. CustomerWhen I come back next week, I want my build where I left it, so the decision can take the time it needs.
Requirements came as a problem statement and brief from Bentley’s product manager, refined in stakeholder sessions, then built in six months.

05What the reviews showed

01

Customers don't know what they want until they see it

A Mulliner spec involves combinations of finishes most people have never seen together. Showing a swatch and a description is not the same as showing the car. The product had to render every choice immediately and unconditionally, no apply button, no preview state, no waiting.

How we knewBentley’s own data on real buyers, brought to us as the problem statement, and the stakeholder sessions that unpacked it: swatches, samples and reference cars were on every showroom floor, and buyers still could not picture their own combination, confidence built over weeks of visits.→ Decision 1

Read fromBentley’s buyer data · the stakeholder sessions that unpacked it
02

Letting customers roam freely didn't help them

The first prototype let users jump between any option in any order. In review, this didn't help anyone: customers got lost, and advisors had to step in to guide. Constraining the experience into a sequence (model → exterior → interior → wheels → personalisation → review) was one of the more important calls in the project, and not the obvious one.

How we knewThe first prototype was free-form. Reviewed with Bentley’s stakeholders against what their buyer data showed, customers get lost without structure and advisors end up coaching, it was replaced by the guided sequence.→ Decision 2

Read fromthe first prototype, reviewed against the buyer data
03

The real output is the build summary, not the screen

What sales advisors valued most wasn't the configurator itself, it was what came out of it: a clean build summary they could hand to the dealership and production team without any translation or rework. The screens exist to produce that document. Once we understood this, sharing stopped being an export feature buried in a menu and became a core surface of the product.

How we knewWorkflow reviews with Bentley’s stakeholders and Mulliner-trained advisors: what mattered downstream was a build summary the dealership and production team could use without translation or rework.→ Decision 3

Read fromworkflow reviews with Mulliner-trained advisors

06The constraint that became the technique

The decision that defined the product came first and was technical: there would be no 3D. It gets its own section because everything after it depends on it.

Decision 1: Real-time visual feedback without 3D

Before

The brief assumed real-time 3D. At Bentley fidelity on showroom iPads that meant loading waits or visible quality loss, and Bentley accepts neither.

After

Every option a flat PNG layer at a fixed position; colour as a fill under a 0.8-opacity detail layer. One body set wears every colour, and choices render at once, on older iPads too.

The original brief assumed a 3D rendering pipeline. After evaluating options, the team concluded that real-time 3D was not viable at the visual fidelity Bentley required. Load times would have broken the experience; reducing fidelity would have broken the brand.

What we didn't do: real-time 3D. Not because it was hard, because it couldn't hit Bentley-grade fidelity on showroom iPads, and Bentley does not accept visible quality loss.

Instead of dropping fidelity, we changed the technique:

  • Every customisable component (body, wheels, interior panels, stitching, trim inlays) rendered as a flat PNG layer at a fixed dimension, with pixel-accurate X/Y positioning derived from a master Photoshop layout
  • Colour works through layering, not asset swaps: the body's detail layer (all the lighting, reflections, and shading) sits at roughly 0.8 opacity over a flat colour fill, so any paint colour shows through while the surface detail stays intact
  • One set of body assets wears every colour in the range

The result felt indistinguishable from a render, loaded immediately, and held up on older iPads.

Tradeoff: the asset production pipeline was heavier than 3D would have required. Each new model meant a new layered Photoshop file, with every option matted out at a consistent vanishing point, across the project this came to more than 1,500 PNG assets, produced and positioned by hand. We absorbed that cost in the design team because it was a one-time investment per model and a permanent gain in runtime quality.
TRY THE TECHNIQUE · LAYERED PNG, NO 3D

One greyscale detail layer (lighting, reflections, shading) at 0.8 opacity over a flat colour. Change the colour; the detail never changes. Slide the opacity to see why 0.8 was the number.

07The other three decisions

With choose-and-see solved, the remaining decisions shaped the experience around it. Each is told as before and after.

Decision 2: A guided sequence, not free exploration

Before

Free exploration in any order, the first prototype. Customers wandered instead of committing, and advisors ended up coaching.

After

Model, exterior, interior, wheels, personalisation, review. Step back any time, never skip ahead; advisors step in at predictable moments.

Free-form configuration was the obvious default, and the one we built first. Review with Bentley’s stakeholders, against what their own buyer data showed, made the case for replacing it: customers who can touch anything spend more time wandering than committing, and the lack of structure pushes advisors into a coaching role they aren’t in the room to perform.

The guided flow (model → exterior → interior → wheels → personalisation → review) gave the experience a rhythm and let advisors step in at predictable moments. We kept the ability to step back through earlier decisions, but removed the ability to skip ahead. The customer always saw the next decision and never lost their place.

Decision 3: Share as a first-class action

Before

Sharing as an export, tucked in a menu at the end of the flow.

After

The primary action of the Review screen: one tap sends a structured summary to the dealer, in the format the build team consumes directly.

Sharing isn't a flourish at the end of the flow; it's the point. The Review screen is where the configurator earns its keep. A finished build generates a structured summary that goes to the dealer as a single tap, in a format the build team can consume directly.

This decision changed the information architecture. Sharing isn't tucked under a menu; it's the primary action of the final screen, and it's why the product exists.

Decision 4: Builds persist across sessions

Before

A build lived for one visit, while a Mulliner sale spans several.

After

A lightweight account and a build history the advisor pulls up at the next meeting, with every choice intact, on the same device or another.

A Mulliner sale spans multiple visits. Builds had to survive between sessions, on the same device or another one. We added a lightweight account model and a build history that an advisor could pull up at the start of the next meeting, with full version state intact.

08The configurator, end to end

How a build moves through the product, from the first model to the dealership. The car never leaves the screen, and the only way out is the build summary.

THE SCREENS, IN ORDER · USE THE ARROWS OR SWIPE
1 / 7

The screen’s contract and the architecture

Information architecture

Home → Browse models → Select model → Visualizer (Exterior → Interior → Wheels → Personalisation) → Review → Share

The visualizer sits at the centre of the product. Every other screen either gets the customer there or handles the artefact it produces.

Interaction principles

The car is always visible. No control covers more than roughly a third of the screen at any time. Choices commit on tap; there is no apply button. Material and colour previews use a single lighting setup so customers can trust the consistency of what they see across selections. We worked within Bentley's brand guidelines, which kept the primary action identical on every screen, customers always know where the next step is.

Constraints we worked within

  • The asset pipeline meant each new model required lead time on Photoshop layering. The information architecture was built to accommodate this, new models slot into the existing category structure without redesign.
  • Showroom connectivity is unreliable. The configurator works offline by default; sharing falls back gracefully when it can't reach a network.

09What we removed

The most valuable part of a luxury digital product is what isn’t on screen. What came out, and what each removal gave back.

  • Real-time 3DReplaced by layered PNGs: the fidelity stayed and the loading went.
  • Free-form navigationReplaced by a five-step sequence: customers stopped wandering, advisors stopped coaching.
  • The apply button and the preview stateEvery choice commits on tap and renders immediately. No gap between choose and see.
  • The swatch-only stateNo option is shown as a swatch on its own; every choice is shown on the customer’s car.
  • Share, buried in a menuIt became the primary action of the final screen.
  • Small buttons and controlsInteractions rebuilt around tap and scroll, the two gestures nobody gets wrong.
  • Nested screensThe navigation hierarchy was flattened after walkthroughs showed people backing out of them.
  • Public availability (later, Bentley’s call)Open access let anyone send casual build requests to dealers. Restricted to executive and showroom use, it went back to serious buyers.

How it was validated

Validation ran in three channels: Bentley’s own buyer data, which arrived with the brief as the problem statement; review sessions with Bentley’s stakeholders, including Mulliner-trained sales advisors; and side-by-side comparisons of interaction variants built and walked through within the team. What it did not include was sessions with end customers: Bentley’s buyers weren’t ours to recruit, and the brief carried their data.

The most consequential review was of the first prototype. Free exploration looked like the obvious design, and against Bentley’s buyer data it reproduced the showroom problem the brief described: without structure the customer wanders and the advisor ends up coaching. The guided sequence was built so that advisors step in at predictable moments instead of narrating throughout, and that argument, not a metric, is what replaced open navigation.

Other iterations from review:

  • The hardest interface problem was fitting the customisation controls onto a compact mobile screen. The option selectors ran edge to edge, and on a small display the early versions felt cramped and fiddly to operate accessibly. We stripped out buttons and small controls wherever possible and rebuilt the interactions around tap and scroll, the two gestures nobody gets wrong. That's why the shipped product has so few visible controls.
  • Navigation hierarchy was simplified after early walkthroughs showed people backing out of nested screens.
  • Visual hierarchy on the review screen was rebuilt to make the share action unmistakable; it had originally been buried as a secondary button.
  • Aligning the layered PNG assets was unforgiving work. Every layer had to sit in exactly the right position, a deviation of even one pixel put a wheel or a trim line visibly out of place and broke the illusion of a single render. Getting each asset set to register perfectly took repeated adjustment rounds between design and engineering.

What changed in practice

The configurator became the default surface for in-showroom Mulliner conversations. The iPad sat between customer and advisor as the shared surface for composing the complete build, working alongside the physical samples on the floor, not replacing them.

Submissions to the build team became uniform. Every build left the room as the same structured summary (the same option codes, the same ordering) which meant less verification work for the production team downstream.

Customers left sessions with a build they had specified themselves rather than a build the advisor had narrated to them. The qualitative shift that mattered most was the decline in requests to physically see a reference car before committing, the configurator was the reference.

Bentley later pulled the app from public availability, for a practical reason: open access meant anyone could send a build request to a dealership, and many of those requests were casual, sent on a whim, with no response when dealers followed up. Restricting the app to executives and showroom use put it back in the hands of serious buyers, in the room where builds are actually specified. It had a second benefit: on showroom iPads, the compact-mobile-screen problem stopped mattering, the interface had the space it worked best at. The move cut off any public-facing metrics, but the product was retained exactly where it earned its keep.

Honest limits on what I can claim

This was an agency engagement, which means I don't have access to post-launch telemetry from Bentley's side. I can speak to the qualitative shifts I observed in stakeholder reviews, advisor workflow reviews and our own walkthroughs; I can't claim a specific completion-rate lift or transaction-time reduction. The numbers I would want (sessions per build, share-to-pricing time, build-to-order conversion) sit on Bentley's side and weren't part of the contractual scope.

A portfolio piece is more useful when it's honest about this than when it borrows credibility from numbers nobody can verify.

Learnings I've taken forward

Real-time visual feedback is the most important single factor in a high-value configurator. Every other usability improvement I made on this project, combined, was smaller than the gain from removing the gap between choose and see.

A performance constraint can become a design technique. The layered-PNG system started as a workaround for an absent 3D pipeline; it ended as a faster, sharper rendering approach than 3D would have given us at this fidelity.

The most valuable part of a luxury digital product is what isn't on screen. Everything we removed (the free-form navigation, the apply button, the swatch-only state, the menu-buried share) contributed more to the experience than anything we added.

01Executive Summary

Market research has always traded depth for scale. Sagan refuses the trade: it's an AI interviewer, it speaks, listens, probes, and follows up, holding a real research conversation with physicians and patients at whatever scale a study needs. ZoomRx has been AI-first from the start; Sagan is that conviction applied to the interview itself.

I designed the interview experience across web and mobile: the conversation and its turn-taking, the captioning system, the switches between spoken and on-screen answers, and the recovery paths for an audience that gets interrupted for a living.

Submission rates and participation increased by ~30% versus text-based formats, measured before and after deployment, and within the year Sagan was a product ZoomRx sells to pharma companies.

02The trade it refuses

Market research offers two bad options. A qualitative interview delivers depth, but needs a trained human moderator, a scheduled call, and budgets that keep samples small. A survey delivers scale, but flattens open answers into typed fragments from respondents racing to finish. The depth-versus-scale tradeoff is structural, and physician time makes it worse: the people whose answers matter most have the least patience for either format.

Because ZoomRx designs the studies itself (the drafts, the paths, the logic) an AI could credibly hold the moderator's chair: the conversation probes freely inside a structure we already know.

Design challenge

How might we make an interview with an AI feel like talking to a good human moderator, for a professional audience with zero patience for friction?

03The interview, as a script

The product is a conversation, so here is one, from the study card on the panel to the moment the payment is initiated. Every line on the left is something a respondent sees or hears; every note on the right is the decision that put it there.

Every screen named here is on the V2 boards, web and mobile. The sample question is the one already shown on this page; the probe is left as a placeholder rather than invented.

04Who is in the conversation

Three parties are in every interview, and only one of them is human on the respondent’s side of the screen. Roles as the brief and the study designs describe them, and the jobs each one needed done.

THE JOBS THE PRODUCT HAD TO DO
  1. Physician respondentWhen I’m talking to an AI moderator, I want to know whose turn it is, so I’m not talking over it or waiting in silence.
  2. Physician respondentWhen the moderator says something long, I want to see what was said, so I don’t have to hold it in my head.
  3. Physician respondentWhen a question involves something to look at, I want it on screen, so I can answer precisely.
  4. Physician respondentWhen life interrupts, I want to step away and come back without losing my place, so the interview survives a real day.
  5. Research teamWhen we need depth at scale, we want a conversation that probes freely inside the structure we designed, so the data is both deep and comparable.
Studies are designed in-house (the drafts, the paths, the logic) so requirements came from the study structures themselves and from the community team that fields them.

05How we knew

Every version was tested end to end, internally, before any physician saw it. The physicians came afterwards, at scale, through the live studies.

RESEARCH & EVIDENCE
Methods
ZoomRx’s own study structures as the starting point · internal UAT, end to end and repeatedly, the design and development team and the community team · pattern borrowing from video and voice conventions (the YouTube-style caption) · the survey platform’s End-of-Survey Feedback on live Sagan studies · a before-and-after comparison of submission and participation around deployment · Claude Code for ideation
Who we learned from
The community team, who own Sagan and field the studies, and the developers, in UAT; then physicians at scale through the live studies and their end-of-survey feedback: Sagan is fielded through the panel platform from the Survey case study
Data
Submission and participation rates, before and after deployment · end-of-survey feedback on Sagan studies · UAT observations, round after round
Not done, and why
No sessions with physicians before launch, the first external respondents were the live studies, and the feedback channel built for the survey platform caught what they thought. Interview counts, drop-off and client specifics stay internal.

06What UAT showed

01

A conversation needs a visible turn-taker

When someone speaks to a machine, the twin anxieties are "did it hear me?" and "should I be talking now?" Every state (listening, processing, moderator speaking) had to be explicit, or respondents talk over the AI, repeat themselves, and trust collapses.

How we knewInternal UAT: the design and development team and the community team ran the interview end to end, repeatedly. Without explicit states, testers talked over the moderator, repeated themselves, or sat waiting for nothing.→ Decision 2

Read frominternal UAT, end to end, repeatedly
02

The screen remembers what sound can't

Spoken words disappear the moment they're said. So the screen keeps the record: captions while the AI talks, and a history of every answer already given. If you missed something or want to check something, it's there.

How we knewThe same UAT rounds, run audio-only first: a missed question had no way back, and in an interview a missed question is a broken answer. Captions followed, then the wall-of-text problem, then the eight-word cap and the history view.→ Decisions 3 and 5

Read fromUAT rounds run audio-only first
03

Some questions need to be seen, not heard

Talking is the richest way to answer "why." But when a question involves something to look at (an ad, a reference image, a set of options to compare) voice alone fails: you can't speak a picture. Those moments move to the screen, and the design had to know which was which, question by question.

How we knewZoomRx’s own study designs: stimulus questions (an ad, a reference image, options to compare) already existed in the studies Sagan would run, and none of them can be spoken.→ Decision 4

Read fromZoomRx’s own study designs

07Five decisions, five moments

Each decision answers one moment where a conversation with a machine breaks.

Decision 1: An interviewer, not a form with a voice

The moment

A respondent gives an interesting answer. A form with a voice would simply read out the next question.

The response

Sagan probes like a good moderator, bounded by the study structure ZoomRx designed, so it digs in without drifting off-study.

What we didn't do: an open-ended chatbot that wanders wherever the respondent takes it, impressive in a demo, indefensible in a recorded research conversation.

Sagan doesn't read a questionnaire aloud, it runs the interview. It introduces itself, asks, listens, and probes with follow-ups the way a good moderator digs into an interesting answer. We could let it do that safely because we design the studies ourselves: the AI probes freely inside a structure whose every path we already know.

Tradeoff: an AI that probes can drift off-study. Bounding it to the research structure gave up some spontaneity, and bought the reliability a recorded medical-adjacent conversation cannot do without.

Decision 2: Whose turn it is, always visible

The moment

The respondent stops talking and nothing happens. Did it hear me? Should I speak? Is it broken?

The response

Every state is named on screen (preparing, connecting, setting up audio, listening, processing) with a persistent indicator of who holds the floor.

A voice conversation fails the moment nobody knows whose turn it is. Every state is explicit: Preparing your interview room. Connecting your moderator. Setting up audio. Listening… Processing your response…, with a persistent indicator showing whether the moderator or you holds the floor. Even the pre-interview sequence is deliberate ritual: it frames what follows as a meeting, not a form.

Tradeoff: more visible machinery than a minimal aesthetic would want. Accepted: in voice, reassurance beats minimalism.
TRY THE STATES · WHOSE TURN IS IT?
PREPARING YOUR INTERVIEW ROOM
Setting up a quiet room for you.
MODERATORYOU

Every state is explicit, and every caption is eight words or fewer. Step through the sequence a respondent actually sees.

Decision 3: Captions, capped at eight words

The moment

The moderator asks something long and the respondent catches half of it. In an interview, a missed question is a broken answer.

The response

Everything Sagan says is captioned, eight words at a time; the respondent’s own speech is never captioned.

What we didn't do: caption the respondent's own speech. Watching your words appear and get interpreted in real time pulls your attention onto the transcription instead of your answer, distracting at best, disorienting when the interpretation lags or misses. Captions run one way only: the AI's side of the conversation.

Everything Sagan says is captioned on screen, and each caption holds a maximum of eight words, so the text stays big enough to read at a glance. Nothing gets missed, with or without sound.

Tradeoff: the cap constrains the writing itself, every question has to be phrased for the ear and for an eight-word screen. Harder to write, easier to follow.

Decision 4: Voice where it's rich, screen where it's precise

The moment

The question is about an ad, a reference image or a 1–6 rating. You cannot speak a picture.

The response

The conversation switches to the screen: a tap for a rating, the image for a stimulus, a checklist with typed input for a multi-select.

Open-ended answers are spoken. But a 1–6 rating is a tap, a stimulus is an image on screen, and a multi-select is a checklist with typed input where the options don't fit. The conversation switches modality to whatever makes the answer most accurate. V2 added the single-select beside them, and kept every option speakable: say it instead of tapping it and the answer is mapped to the nearest option on screen, mispronounced or not.

Tradeoff: switching between speaking and tapping mid-conversation risks breaking the flow, the turn-taking states exist partly to make those hand-offs feel natural.

Decision 5: The interview survives real life

The moment

A patient walks in mid-interview. A linear interview would punish exactly the busy respondents the research wants most.

The response

Sagan notices the silence, asks “Are you there?”, offers a break and saves progress; on return it recaps before continuing.

Clinicians get interrupted. Sagan notices silence ("Are you there?"), offers breaks, saves progress, and when the respondent returns, it recaps what was already discussed before continuing. The interview ends properly too: completion, the honorarium payment initiated, and a transcript-style history the respondent can revisit. The panel card carries the way back too: the time remaining and Continue interview, so a paused interview is never lost in the dashboard.

Tradeoff: an interruptible interview is more work to design than a linear one. But an interview that punishes interruption would select against exactly the busy, senior respondents the research wants most.

The interview shipped three times before its look was redone a fourth. The developers’ base came first, then two designed versions, each tested end to end in UAT before any physician saw it; the restyle closes this page.

V2 · MOBILE · THE SAME ARC, PLUS THE APP PROMPT
