The thread that ran through them

Two problems were the hardest, and both came from the same place: in an AI interview, the user gets lost easily.

The first: whose turn is it? Every version was tested end to end in UAT, the design and development team and the community team, round after round, before any physician saw it. In early versions, testers couldn't tell when the AI was speaking, when it was their turn, or why there was silence while the AI prepared a follow-up. Every one of those gaps broke the conversation: people talked over the moderator, repeated themselves, or sat waiting for nothing. Defining the full set of states (moderator speaking, listening, processing, preparing the next question) was the most complicated design work in the product, precisely because human conversation makes turn-taking invisible and an AI conversation has to make it explicit.

The second: how much should the screen say while the AI speaks?

  • We started audio-only: the purest version of a conversation. It had a real flaw: if a respondent misses something the AI said, there's no way to recover it, and in an interview, a missed question is a broken answer.
  • So we added closed captions. But a wall of text pulls attention away from listening and quietly turns the conversation back into reading.
  • The answer was YouTube-style captioning: short lines, a maximum of eight words at a time: big, glanceable, gone. Enough to catch what you missed, never enough to compete with the voice.
  • And for anything beyond the moment, the history state: recall any answer already given, so nothing depends on memory.

That sequence, audio-only → captions → capped captions + history, is the product's learning, in shipped form. And the two threads together, the turn-taking states and the caption system, are why the interview feels effortless: the hardest work in the product is the machinery you barely notice.

09The interview, end to end

The interview, end to end

Profile verification → the study card with its honorarium → guidance (find a quiet spot; don't share personally identifying information) → the room-preparation sequence → the conversation → completion, payment initiated, dashboard. One arc, identical across web and mobile, the interview is the product on both.

The history state

A transcript-style view lets respondents recall every answer they've given. The conversation is never a black box, and stepping away never means losing your place.

Sagan Agents: the platform the interview seeded

What changed in practice

Submission rates and participation increased by ~30% versus text-based formats, the format, not respondent willingness, was the constraint. Now sold to pharma companies as a ZoomRx product, the commercial answer arrived fast: work began in 2025, the product reached the market in 2026, and from zero it now brings ZoomRx about $2 million a year from paying clients.

It also outgrew its starting point. Sagan has since grown into Sagan Agents: ZoomRx's agentic operating system for pharma insights, spanning archive intelligence, agentic market research, and strategic insights agents, which is what the project link now opens. The respondents’ own verdict comes through the survey platform’s end-of-survey feedback on live Sagan studies, where HCPs describe the interviews as concise, straightforward and well-directed. The interview experience I designed is where that platform began.

Honest limits on what I can claim

ZoomRx work: the 30% figure is the shareable headline, measured as a before-and-after comparison around deployment. Underlying data, interview counts, revenue and client specifics were shared internally and stay internal.

Learnings I've taken forward

Changing how people answer, speaking instead of typing, moved the results more than years of refining what they were asked. The input method turned out to be the biggest design lever in the product, bigger than any screen-level improvement.

The principles Sagan Agents now markets as human-in-the-loop (a process you can see, a conversation you can intervene in, answers you can trace) were in the interview's DNA from the start: visible turn-taking, bounded probing, a history you can always check. Designing trust into the first product turned out to be designing the philosophy of the platform.

The logomark is built from three ideas, an intelligence loop, noise resolving into clarity and workflows, drawn as four bars on a hairline; the palette is stone, yellow, near-black and cream; Libre Bodoni carries the headings and Geist the product UI. An AI intelligence platform for life sciences, designing how AI answers high-stakes pharma questions, before the industry had patterns for any of it.

01Executive Summary

Pharma strategy runs on questions: which trials read out, what a competitor's pipeline holds, how a drug performed, what happened at a conference. The teams asking (competitive intelligence, business development, medical affairs) used to pay for answers in analyst-days. Ferma answers in seconds, with the evidence attached. The product began as Ferma Chat, built after the LLM wave alongside Ferma’s conference-coverage product, and is called Ferma Agents today.

I designed how it answers. The response system that turns AI output into something a pharma analyst can defend (structured clinical answers, visible sources, comparison tables) and the harder second act: the argument that a chat box was the wrong container for research, and the design of the workspace it should become. Along the way: the collaboration layer, both light and dark themes, and the mobile version.

The timing is the point. This was built in the early ChatGPT era, when nothing was settled, how an AI answer should look, how sources should show, what happens when a question is too big. Every convention had to be decided from first principles, and the boards record those decisions being made.

Ferma is today a dedicated ZoomRx business unit, publicly positioned as the AI pharma intelligence platform and, per its own site, trusted by 100+ leading biopharma companies. The answering experience I designed is where it began.

02An answer nobody knew how to draw

Life-sciences teams sit on enormous, fragmented information: trial results, competitive moves, regulatory events, conference intelligence. Getting an answer meant knowing which source held it and having the time to dig. Generic large language models offered speed but failed the domain: a confident answer with a wrong drug name is worse than a slow answer.

And underneath that sat the design problem with no borrowed solution: nobody knew what an AI answer to a clinical question should look like. Not how long, not how structured, not how sourced, not what to do when the question returns three thousand results. The interface conventions didn't exist. We had to design them.

Design challenge

How should an AI answer a question when the person asking is paid to be right, and no design conventions exist yet?

03Who asks, and what they need

Four teams ask, and every one of them is paid to be right. Roles, not invented people, and the jobs each one needed the product to do.

THE JOBS THE PRODUCT HAD TO DO
  1. CI analystWhen I ask a clinical question, I want the answer to show where it came from, so I can quote it in a client report.
  2. BD&L analystWhen I compare trials or assets, I want them side by side with sources attached, so comparison is an operation, not copy-and-paste.
  3. Any analystWhen my question is too vague or too big, I want help shaping it, so I don’t get three thousand results, or nothing.
  4. Any analystWhen research spans days, I want my findings to accumulate, so I’m not pasting answers into documents to keep them.
  5. TeamWhen a colleague has done the work, we want to share it with the right permissions, so AI research becomes a team asset.
Requirements came from the problems analysts hit using it, and, for the workspace, from the document I wrote proposing what Ferma should become.

04How we knew

The first users sat inside ZoomRx, and the product listened through every answer it gave.

RESEARCH & EVIDENCE
Methods
Working alongside ZoomRx’s own analysts as the first users · feedback from business-development team members at pharma companies using it · side-by-side benchmarking against ChatGPT and Perplexity · the per-response feedback control shipped in the product · options compared on the boards before choosing, four sources-panel layouts, the truncation alternatives
Who we learned from
ZoomRx’s own analysts and consultants, people who quote answers in reports clients read, and BD team members at pharma companies; the consulting team inside the project
Data
Per-response feedback on live answers · what analysts did with answers (copying pieces into documents) · generic-model failures on domain questions, a confident answer with a wrong drug name · the boards’ option comparisons
Not done, and why
No formal usability programme with external users, the first users were in-house analysts, and the product’s own feedback control did the listening. Performance data and client specifics stay inside ZoomRx.

05What the first analysts taught us

01

Expert users don't want answers; they want defensible answers

An analyst quotes Ferma's output in reports read by clients. Every response needed a visible chain back to evidence: the interface had to support verification as a first-class behaviour, not a footnote.

How we knewZoomRx’s own analysts, who quote answers in client reports, and the benchmark against ChatGPT and Perplexity: a confident generic answer with a wrong drug name is worse than a slow one.→ Calls 1 and 2

Read fromin-house analysts and the ChatGPT / Perplexity benchmark
02

Asking is easy in chat; research isn't

A chat flow answers one question at a time. Real research is non-linear: analysts follow several paths, abandon some, come back to old insights and connect them. Constrained to chat alone, they were manually copying pieces of answers into documents to use later. The product had to become a place where research accumulates, not just a place where questions get answered.

How we knewWorking alongside the in-house analysts: constrained to chat, they were copying pieces of answers into documents to use later, the behaviour that argued for a workspace.→ Call 5

Read fromworking alongside the in-house analysts
03

The question itself is a design problem

An empty search bar is intimidating when the question isn't framed yet, and a badly scoped question returns three thousand results nobody can use. The design had to help on both ends: suggesting what to ask before typing, and helping narrow the ask when it came back too big.

How we knewAn empty search bar when the question isn’t framed yet, and three thousand results when it is too broad, both seen with the first analysts using it.→ Call 3

Read fromthe first analysts using it

06Anatomy of an answer

Every chatbot of the time streamed prose. For a clinical question that is the wrong object: nobody can scan it, and nobody can defend it. So the answer became something designed, with an anatomy per kind of ask and the same things on every one of them: citation chips, the sources panel, feedback and copy.

07The decision log

No patterns existed to borrow, so the decisions were made on the boards, with the options they beat drawn beside them. Five calls, as logged.

Call 1: The answer is a designed object, not generated text

CALL 01 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD

How should an AI answer to a clinical question look?

On the table, not taken
Free-form prose, streamed as it is generatedThe default every chatbot shipped with: unscannable and unverifiable for clinical content.
The call
One designed anatomy per ask-type, with a narrative fallback

Instead, every answer type got a designed anatomy. Structured summaries with named fields (Efficacy, Safety, Drug, Indications) where the ask was specific; narrative layouts with a strict typographic hierarchy where it was open-ended; long answers split into short points with a background summary up top and drug names bolded; multi-result answers as collapsed cards, with the truncation call recorded on the board at the moment it was made: show the collapsed view, one field visible.

Tradeoff: every format is a template, and a template can mis-fit an answer. We carried formats per ask-type plus a narrative fallback, more design surface to maintain, in exchange for answers an analyst can scan in seconds and defend in a meeting.

Call 2: Evidence lives inside the answer

CALL 02 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD

Where do the sources live?

On the table, not taken
An appendix under the answer
The call
Inside the answer: citation chips on every claim-carrying block, and a sources panel
THE PANEL ITSELF: FOUR LAYOUTS, COMPARED SIDE BY SIDE BEFORE CHOOSING
Paginated at five
Paginated at ten
Scrolling
Scrolling plus pagination

Sources are part of the response, not an appendix: citation chips on every claim-carrying block, and a sources panel, fifty references deep when it had to be, with search built in. We explored the panel's form deliberately: paginated at five, at ten, scrolling, scrolling-plus-pagination, laid side by side and compared before choosing. The design bet underneath it all: for this audience, verifiability is usability.

Tradeoff: denser responses and slower reading than a clean chat bubble. Accepted: the audience is paid to verify.

Call 3: When the question is too big or too vague, the AI helps shape it

CALL 03 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD

What happens when a question is too big, or not framed yet?

On the table, not taken
Return three thousand results and call it an answer
The call
Explain the scope problem and offer ways to narrow; suggest questions before anything is typed

Broad questions got a designed response of their own: the AI explains the scope problem and offers tailored ways to narrow (by category, time period, specific study, demographic, outcome) written as help, with concrete example questions. And before any question is typed, the empty state suggests what's worth asking, because a blank box is a wall when the question isn't framed yet.

Tradeoff: declining to answer risks feeling unhelpful. The nudges had to read as "here's how to get what you actually want", a copywriting and tone problem as much as an interface one, with response templates written and rewritten for exactly that.

The same idea, scoping the question before it is answered, grew into focus areas. A focus area holds the firms, drugs, indications, drug classes, targets and development stages a team cares about, and refines every conversation until it is switched; switching starts a new chat, so answers never mix two scopes.

Call 4: Comparison as a first-class operation

CALL 04 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD

How do two trials get compared?

On the table, not taken
A paragraph that describes both
The call
A table: named rows, two entities side by side, sources attached
AND ITS FIRST ITERATION, FROM THE ANALYSTS USING IT
Before
Expand, one truncated cell at a timeToo many clicks, the analysts said.
After
Expand Content opens every cell at onceThe old Expand became Fullscreen, so the two could not be confused.

Analysts compare things for a living, trials, drugs, readouts. So comparison isn't a paragraph; it's a table: named rows (Phase, Enrollment, Arms, Efficacy, Safety, Conclusion), two entities side by side, sources attached. And the table earned its own iteration from real feedback: expanding truncated cells one by one was too many clicks, so we added Expand Content to open them all at once, and renamed the old Expand to Fullscreen so the two couldn't be confused.

Tradeoff: tables inside a conversation break the chat metaphor. Accepted without hesitation: the metaphor serves the analyst, not the other way round.

Call 5: Beyond the chat: research as the container

CALL 05 · AS LOGGED ON THE BOARD

What container does research need?

On the table, not taken
Keep bolting features onto the chat
The call
A workspace: tasks and profiles, an orchestrator, spaces where findings accumulate; chat stays how you ask

As the product matured, I wrote the argument that the chat paradigm itself was the ceiling, a document proposing what Ferma should become: workflows and tasks as the core concept, with agent selection removed as a user burden (an orchestrator routes to agents invisibly); profiles (business development, competitive intelligence, scientific communications, new product planning) each carrying pre-built key tasks; and spaces where highlighted responses, insights, and charts accumulate per goal, get compared and tracked, and turn into shareable reports. Chat remains how you ask; the workspace is where research lives.

Tradeoff: proposing a structural change is slower and riskier than shipping the next feature, it has to convince people before it can exist. That's why it was written down, with the flows designed alongside the argument.

The board kept the score

The design boards are themselves the validation record, decisions were made in public, on the canvas, with their reasoning attached:

  • Options explored side by side before choosing, the sources panel's four layout variants, the summary truncation alternatives
  • Decisions written where they were made: "DECISION: show the collapsed view, one field truncated" sits on the board next to the options it beat
  • Iterations traceable to feedback: Expand Content exists because the analysts using it said expanding cells one by one was too many clicks; the old button was renamed Fullscreen in the same stroke
  • A feedback loop shipped in the product: every response carries its own feedback control, so the answer formats kept learning from the people using them

08Beyond the chat

Call 5 was not a feature. It was an argument that the container was wrong, written down because it had to convince people before it could exist. Here it is drawn.

Sharing AI work, before anyone had a pattern for it

Research that accumulates is research a team wants to share. Explorer and Viewer roles, team-gated access, a library of shared chats, and sharing to the team kept apart from sharing in public: collaboration patterns for AI conversations, designed while the conversations themselves were still new.

09Conventions invented on the way

Designing where no patterns existed

This is the section other case studies can't have, because the work happened before the conventions did. What the boards show being invented, decision by decision:

How a clinical answer should readthe field-based and narrative formats, the two-sentence-point rule for long answers, background summaries first, the typographic hierarchy
How evidence should attachcitation chips, the sources panel, and the compared layout options that chose its final form
What to do at the edgesthe too-vague question (suggested asks) and the too-big answer (designed narrowing)
How teams share AI workExplorer and Viewer roles, team-gated access, shared-chat libraries, share-to-team versus public: collaboration patterns for AI conversations before anyone had them
The unglamorous completenessfull skeleton-loading systems in both light and dark themes, per-response feedback, copy states, and a designed mobile version

From wireframe to platform

The boards also hold the arc: early light-theme wireframes evolving into the shipped dark-theme product, the theming system that kept both alive, and the workspace direction pointing at what came next. The product's history is legible in its own design files.

What changed in practice

Questions that cost analyst-days became questions that cost seconds, answered in formats built to be scanned, compared, and defended, with the evidence one glance away. The response conventions designed here became the product's foundation, and the workspace argument shaped where it went next.

The public arc says the rest. Ferma is today a dedicated ZoomRx business unit with its own platform family, conference intelligence and agentic workflows, publicly positioned against the industry's incumbent data platforms and, per its own site, trusted by 100+ leading biopharma companies. The answering experience I designed is where it began.

Honest limits on what I can claim

Ferma is ZoomRx work. Specific performance data and client details stay inside ZoomRx; this case study describes the design reasoning at the level I can share.

Learnings I've taken forward

Designing AI products for expert users inverts the usual instinct: the goal isn't hiding complexity, it's exposing exactly the right complexity, the evidence, at the right moment.

And the bigger one: when the container is wrong, the senior move is to say so in writing. The workspace document argued that a chat box couldn't carry real research, with a designed alternative attached. Formats and screens age; the willingness to challenge the paradigm you're working inside is the skill that transfers everywhere.

11The design system

Ferma runs on one system in two themes. Blue leads, nine dark shades build the surfaces, greys carry the borders and lines, and the accents are kept for illustrations and alternative states; Nunito Sans sets everything. Every component was drawn state by state, default, hover, click and disabled, in dark mode and again in light. Here it is rebuilt on the page from the design file.

DESIGNING WITH AGENTSIN USE · SPI TEAM

Boilerplate Generator

Packaging a design system as an agent skill, then building the pipeline that uses it: a survey draft in, reviewed on-brand screens out, graded against a rubric before a human ever sees them.

IN 10 SECONDS
PROBLEMEvery survey needs the same instructional screens designed again, by hand, at a quality no one could hold steady.
EVIDENCEFourteen real survey drafts parsed by the pipeline itself, four working sessions with the design lead, and the output format checked by pasting it into the live survey platform.
BUILTA design system as a machine-readable skill, a corpus-derived screen taxonomy, and an orchestrated designer–evaluator loop with human gates.
STATUSIn use. The SPI team, who build the surveys, now turn a draft into reviewed boilerplate screens in about an hour; it used to take three teams around seven days.
MY ROLESenior Product Designer, ZoomRx, I own the design side: the design system skill, the screen taxonomy, the emphasis rule and the evaluator's rubric. Architecture and review with a design-leadership partner; the pipeline itself is Claude Code plugins and sub-agents I specced and dog-fooded.
OverviewEvidenceInsightsReversalsScreensRulesMachineRunStatus

The design question underneath: what has to exist before a machine can produce work a designer would sign off on?

RoleSenior Product Designer, ZoomRx: design system, taxonomy, rubric, pipeline spec
PlatformClaude Code plugin: skills, sub-agents, an MCP asset server
StatusIn use by the SPI team; eight canonical screens frozen, design and token skills derived from them; dog-fooded over 14 real drafts
TeamMe on the design side, with a design-leadership partner on architecture and review

Most of this case study is a judgement call about where design belongs in an automated pipeline, and one reversal I had to accept.

67in-scope boilerplates, pulled from 14 real survey drafts by the pipeline’s own parsing step
76%of them are Statements: one short paragraph on a card. Get that screen right and most output is right
~1 hrfrom a survey draft to reviewed boilerplate screens, by the SPI team alone. It used to take three teams around seven days

01Executive Summary

A ZoomRx survey draft arrives as a Word document of roughly a hundred questions. Between those questions sit the boilerplates: the instructional, orienting and transition screens that tell a physician what is about to happen. They are not questions, they carry no data, and they get designed by hand for every study, which means they are the first thing to slip when a team is busy. Getting them built took three teams and around seven days per survey.

I built two things. First, the ZoomRx MR design system packaged as a skill: tokens, components, icons and golden structures written so a model can compose a screen without guessing values. Then the Boilerplate Generator, a plugin that reads a draft, decides which boilerplates are worth designing, drafts each one, and has a second agent grade it against a rubric until it clears a bar, with a human gating both the selection and the final output.

  • A design system expressed as primitive → semantic → component tokens, because semantic naming is what makes a system legible to a model
  • A screen taxonomy derived from the real corpus, not from intuition
  • A designer–evaluator loop deliberately made adversarial
  • A rubric where fidelity and emphasis are pass/fail, not matters of taste

The result: the SPI team, the team that builds the surveys, now does it alone, in about an hour.

The version before this one worked and was still wrong: one context window did everything, so long runs blew the window and the model started emitting nonsense. A run took around 30 minutes and ~110k tokens for 7–10 boilerplates, the sub-agents were improvised at runtime so behaviour drifted between runs, and the evaluator accepted work with "only trivial nitpicks", a judgement call dressed as a standard. We restarted from a clean slate, carrying the design intent and nothing else.

02The screens nobody designs

Boilerplates are the easiest screens in the product and the most repeated. Hand-designing them does not scale, but automating them naively produces the thing every designer fears: output that is technically on-brand and visibly wrong, an illustration forced onto a one-sentence screen, a drug name shouting in a pill, a paragraph quietly reworded by a model that thought it could write better than the regulator-approved source.

The real opportunity was not speed. It was the quality floor: if the system can hold a bar without a designer in the loop for every screen, then the designer's time moves to the screens that deserve it.

Design challenge

How might a pipeline produce screens a designer would sign off on, when no designer will look at most of them?

03Who it serves

Four people stand around every generated screen, and only one of them is a designer.

THE JOBS THE PRODUCT HAD TO DO
  1. Product designerWhen a study needs forty boilerplate screens, I want them generated to the bar I’d sign off, so my time goes to the screens that deserve it.
  2. Reviewing designerWhen the output is wrong, I want to say so in plain language and have the pipeline try again, so review is a conversation, not a rebuild.
  3. Study authorWhen a boilerplate is regulator-approved copy, I want it reproduced exactly, so no model rewords it.
  4. Research opsWhen a draft comes in, I want to confirm scope before anything is designed, so the cheapest error is caught first.
  5. Design leadWhen the generator runs on Tuesday, I want the same result as Monday, so the system is repeatable, not merely successful.
Requirements live in the repository itself: an architecture spec, a skills-and-briefs spec, four revisions of written history, and a feedback log of objections as they were raised.

04How we knew

The pipeline produced its own evidence: its parsing step built the corpus the design layer stands on, and every revision was argued through in a working session.

RESEARCH & EVIDENCE
Methods
Dog-fooding the pipeline’s own parsing step over 14 real drafts to build the corpus · classifying the 67 in-scope boilerplates from first principles into a design taxonomy · review of V1 output · four working sessions with a design-leadership partner, objections logged as they were raised · evaluator scorecards from the designer–evaluator loop · the output format verified against the live survey platform
Who we learned from
Myself as the first user of every revision, and a design-leadership partner in four working sessions and a written feedback log
Who else has run it so far, the other designer, research ops? Roughly how many runs?
Data
The corpus: 67 in-scope boilerplates from 14 drafts, of which 51 Statements (76%), 6 Structured Lists, 4 Asset Hand-offs, 4 Composites, 2 Comparison Matrices · V1’s run costs: ~30 minutes and ~110k tokens for 7–10 boilerplates · evaluator scores, 0–2 per dimension
Not done, and why
No usage analytics yet. The before and after (three teams and around seven days, against the SPI team alone in about an hour) are approximate figures, as the team reports them.

05What the first versions taught us

01

A model can't use a design system it has to interpret

The first version derived its visual rules from the legacy codebase and from the draft text. That produced values without meaning. The fix was to build the design system as a skill first: three token tiers where the semantic layer carries the role (text.primary, surface.canvas, button.primary) rather than the value, so an agent picks tokens by intent instead of copying hexes. The same repository holds the icon library, the illustrations and golden structures, so an agent composing a screen has the real inventory rather than a description of it.

How we knewReviewing V1 output: values derived from the legacy codebase and the draft text carried no meaning, so the agent copied hexes instead of choosing by intent.→ the skill’s three token tiers

Read fromreviewing V1 output
02

Design has to come from a canvas, not from a paragraph

This is the lesson I most had to be argued into. I kept deriving design from the source text: read the boilerplates, infer the patterns, write the token set, and let the screens follow. My design-leadership partner's position was the opposite, design the screens on a canvas first, react to them, and derive the rule set afterwards. He was right. The text-derived layer asserted visual opinions ("one white card") that nobody had designed or reacted to, and was internally inconsistent, it cited three different boilerplate counts in three sections of the same document. We retired it and rebuilt top-down.

How we knewA design-leadership partner’s critique across four working sessions, logged as it was raised: the text-derived layer asserted visual opinions nobody had designed and contradicted itself on boilerplate counts. Retired, rebuilt top-down from eight screens designed on the canvas.→ The two reversals

Read fromfour working sessions with the design lead
03

An evaluator that shares the designer's criteria will rubber-stamp it

The first loop had the designer and the evaluator grading by the same criteria on the same model, which is not a review: it is a model approving its own reasoning. Divergence had to be designed in deliberately, a different model, criteria the designer is never told to optimise for, and a scorecard rather than a verdict.

How we knewThe first loop’s results: a designer and an evaluator grading on the same criteria, on the same model, approved each other’s work, “only trivial nitpicks”.→ Decisions 2 and 3

Read fromthe first loop’s results

06Two reversals before the first screen

Four revisions and two reversals came before the first screen was designed. Both reversals were mine to accept, and both taught the same thing from different directions: the rules come after the design, never before it.

REV 1

An architecture reset

Three agents, not four: I proposed folding brief writing into the classifier, and the extra agent was dropped. One overall brief per study plus a thin brief per boilerplate; audience came out of the briefs because the copy and the design never change with it.

REV 2

The architecture as files

The agreed design turned into real agent and skill files: three sub-agents and five skills, each declared once.

REV 3 · REVERSAL

Design derived from text

I wrote the orchestrator and parsing skills for real, then derived a token set and a pattern document from the legacy codebase and the draft text. It asserted “one white card” that nobody had designed or reacted to, and cited three different boilerplate counts in three sections.

WHAT IT TAUGHTRetired. A rule written from text is an opinion nobody has looked at. Design has to be reacted to on a canvas first.
REV 4

The corpus

The parsing step, run over 14 real drafts, pulled out 67 in-scope boilerplates with their verbatim text. Classified from first principles, they reduced to eight canonical screens.

FIRST PASS · REVERSAL

AI renders of the eight

I generated the eight in three AI design tools as a starting point. The review was blunt: “We are skipping over the most important part, which is the expression of your design judgment.” The renders had no real content either.

WHAT IT TAUGHTSent back. Design all eight by hand, on one canvas, with real copy from the corpus and the product’s own colours.
THE CANVAS

Eight screens, designed and frozen

Designed with real boilerplate text, reviewed, then frozen as the source of truth: the target the designer agent aims at and the standard the evaluator grades against.

DERIVED

Then the rules

Primitive tokens exported from the frozen file; the semantic layer, the composition skill and the emphasis rendering derived from the screens; a V0 rubric; and the output format checked against the live survey platform.

Dog-fooding was the useful move: the parsing skill had to work well enough to produce the corpus that the design layer is built on, so the pipeline validated one of its own parts before anything downstream existed.

07The eight screens

These eight are the golden reference for everything the pipeline produces. They are bundled inside the design skill, so the designer agent composes toward them and the evaluator grades against the same eight. Everything else in the project, the tokens, the composition rules, the emphasis rendering and the rubric, is derived from them. Each carries its share of the 67 boilerplates in the corpus.

Why eight, and why these eight

Rather than guess which layouts were needed, I ran the parsing step across 14 real drafts to pull out 67 in-scope boilerplates with their verbatim text, then classified that corpus from first principles. It collapsed into five compositional archetypes (Statement, Structured List, Asset Hand-off, Composite, Comparison Matrix) and the distribution settled the priorities: 76% are Statements, a single short paragraph on a card. Get that one screen right and three-quarters of all output is right.

Functional intent (inform, instruct, prepare, orient, transition) does not drive layout, so it became a second axis that tunes tone, emphasis and whether an illustration is allowed at all. Density became a third. Five archetypes across those axes reduce to roughly eight canonical screens and a component inventory of about fifteen blocks.

Illustration only where it orients

Illustrations come from ZoomRx’s own brand-asset library, reached through an MCP server: the designer agent searches it, picks an asset and references it by its address, and it is the only agent given that connection, so the evaluator judges the choice without having made it. The rule is strict and ordered: an illustration if one genuinely fits, otherwise an icon, otherwise nothing; never a decorative “close enough”. Only screens that orient or prepare may carry one, centred above the text; definitions, transitions and dense screens stand on typography. The evaluator scores an off-topic image as a zero.

08From screen to rule

Here is one screen followed all the way down: what was designed, the semantic tokens it became, and the HTML the designer agent has to emit for the survey platform to accept it.

Why the third column looks like that. Pasted into the live survey platform, the HTML field kept nothing but inline styles: no style block, no variables, no media queries, no head or body. So the designer agent reasons in semantic tokens and writes their literal values inline, and the rubric scores any style block as a hard fail.

One emphasis rule, because bold means three different things

Draft writers have one emphasis tool in Word, so bold arrives carrying three different intents. Treating them identically, the earlier behaviour, turned every screen into a field of pills. The rule separates them: a drug or molecule name is an entity and takes a tag; a therapeutic area is a descriptor and stays in the sentence as inline bold; a placeholder takes a tag with its brackets visible, so dynamic content reads as dynamic; instructional words like CURRENTLY and DO NOT take inline bold; line-of-therapy notation and generic phrases take nothing. It also caps itself: one or two indications in bold per screen, and more than six drug tags means the layout is wrong, not the rule.

One divergence is still open, and the skills say so. The rule asks for an entity tag visibly different from a placeholder tag; on the frozen screens both are the same light monospace tag, told apart only by the brackets. The skills follow the screens, because the screens are the source of truth, and the call is flagged as mine to make.

09The machine around the screens

The screens are the design; this is the machinery that holds them steady from one boilerplate to the next and one run to the next.

Decision 1: An orchestrator with specced sub-agents, not one clever session

What we didn't do: keep improving the single-session version. It worked, which is exactly why it was hard to abandon.

The orchestrator became a conductor: it runs the pipeline, holds the human conversation, spawns sub-agents and reads their short reports, and never does the heavy work itself, so its context stays lean. Three sub-agents (brief writer, designer, evaluator) each run in their own context window and are defined as files, with their model, tools, scope and persona declared once. Because each is specced once and reused, the designer behaves identically across every boilerplate and every run.

Tradeoff: more moving parts and a real specification burden up front, in exchange for runs that are repeatable instead of merely successful. Parallel designers also multiply token cost per minute, the win is wall-clock time and clean context, not spend.

Decision 2: Scope each agent's knowledge asymmetrically

Who gets which skill became a design decision rather than a configuration detail. The brief writer gets the draft-parsing and study-type knowledge. The designer gets the tokens, the composition rules and the brand-asset server. The evaluator gets the same tokens and canonical screens, so it grades against the same target the designer aimed at, plus the rubric and a set of "look out for" criteria the designer never sees, on a different model.

Tradeoff: the asymmetry costs duplication and makes the system harder to explain. It is the only thing keeping the review honest.

Decision 3: A rubric with non-negotiables, not a verdict

The evaluator scores each dimension 0, 1 or 2 and must attach an actionable critique to anything below a 2. A screen passes only when no dimension scores zero and source-text fidelity and emphasis correctness each score a full 2. Those two are correctness, not quality: the visible text must be an in-order subsequence of the source, with nothing added, removed, reordered or rephrased. The remaining dimensions: typography and token compliance, cohesion with the canonical screens, illustration relevance, and consistency with the screens already approved in that run, can carry a partial.

Tradeoff: a rigid gate will fail work a human would have waved through. That is the point: the alternative is "only trivial nitpicks", which is how the first version let bad screens pass.

The architecture, problem by problem

The rebuild started from a written architecture, and its first table is a list of eight things wrong with the version that worked. Every part of the new pipeline answers one of them.

What was wrongWhat it causedWhat the rebuild does
1 · One context window did everythingOn long runs the window blew out and the model emitted nonsense.An orchestrator that only conducts, and three sub-agents with a context window each.
2 · No real agent filesSub-agents were improvised at runtime, so behaviour drifted from run to run.Each agent is a file, specced once: model, tools, scope, persona, skills.
3 · A linear pipelineAbout 30 minutes and 110k tokens for 7 to 10 boilerplates.One designer per boilerplate, in parallel, with evaluation pipelined behind them.
4 · The strongest model on rote workIdentification and file creation ran slow and expensive.Sonnet for brief writing and evaluation; Opus for the design itself.
5 · A subjective evaluator“Only trivial nitpicks” let bad output pass.A rubric with thresholds and two non-negotiables.
6 · A second scoring pass after the loopTwo evaluators, one of them checking what the other ignored.One evaluator, holding every check.
7 · Designer and evaluator on the same criteriaThe evaluator rubber-stamped the designer.Evaluator-only rubric and look-out-for criteria, on a different model.
8 · Draft to markdown by reasoningA solved conversion treated as a model task.A deterministic script, no model at all.

Parallel designers raise one more problem: each one makes its own choices, and a survey’s screens could drift apart. It is solved upstream rather than by going back to one designer: rigid skills with the eight screens as a shared target, the same designer spec for every boilerplate, one overall brief every designer reads, and an evaluator that catches what is left. The input stays the Word draft the SPI team already has, and business context comes from the brief writer’s persona, a pharmaceutical market research expert, rather than a skill nobody could have written yet.

Where the humans stand

Two gates, both deliberate. The first is after classification: a human confirms which boilerplates are in scope before anything is designed, because the cheapest error to fix is a screen that should never have been drafted. The second is after the loop: a human reviews the finished screens and, if they are wrong, says so in plain language, and the orchestrator re-enters the loop with that feedback as context. The outer loop is written into the orchestrator rather than left to the person's initiative.

What the system refuses to do

A sizeable set of boilerplates is deliberately out of scope: consent and privacy screens, anything ending in a yes/no attestation, adverse-event terminology, screen-in and screen-out copy, welcome and post-survey screens. These are detected and skipped rather than attempted. Knowing what not to automate was as much of the design work as the rest.

It found five in-scope boilerplates and named what it left out; a human approved the list at the gate; the designer and the evaluator built and checked the five screens; all five passed. The draft going in is the first image on this page; the four steps after it are below. At the time of this run, the check on the live survey platform was still to come.

Where it stands today

The eight canonical screens are designed and frozen, and the composition and token skills are now derived from them, the top-down order the reversal in section 03 argued for. The pipeline is specified end to end, the orchestrator and parsing skills are written, the three agents are authored, the corpus and taxonomy are the agreed source of truth, the emphasis rule is written and the rubric exists in V0 with six dimensions. The output format has been verified against the live survey platform, which strips everything but inline styles. And it runs end to end: the SPI team uses it on its own, and work that involved three teams and around seven days takes about an hour.

Honest limits on what I can claim

The outcome I can claim is the process change: three teams and around seven days became the SPI team alone and about an hour. Those are approximate figures, as the team reports them, with no usage analytics behind them yet. Everything else here is reasoning I can show: the corpus counts, the old version's costs as the baseline, and the output format checked against the live platform.

Learnings I've taken forward

Design first, derive second: a rule set extracted from text asserts opinions nobody has reacted to. Design the screens, then write the rules the screens imply.

Automation does not remove design judgement; it relocates it. Every decision a designer would normally make per screen has to be made once, in advance, and written down precisely enough for a machine: what emphasis means, when an illustration is allowed, what "good" scores. The rubric is the design work. And a system that reviews itself needs that review to be genuinely adversarial (different model, different criteria, scorecard not verdict) or it will simply agree with itself.
